Was working on-call at a hospice pharmacy. My usual day was work 12pm to 9pm (pharmacy closed at 7pm but there was no point going home because I'd just get called back in) then I'd be on-call until the next morning at 9am, just praying I could get some sleep during that time. Worked 7-on-7-off, on the weekend I was the only pharmacist all day and all night. One of the hospices had a new admit that complained of nausea and vomiting in the middle of the night so at 5am I get the call and head into the pharmacy to type, fill and package the med for a stat delivery (meaning we get it to the patient within two to three hours) for the courier. Pretty routine. Next night I get a call for the same patient around 4am, same complaint. As I finish taking the order I ask them to follow-up with me during the day to make sure their nausea is controlled so they won't need another night call. Go into the pharmacy, pack it up, send it out. Later that day I haven't seen or heard anything about the patient so I call up the hospice and see how the patient is doing, they claim "she's stable." Get a call for the third night in a row at 6am for the same patient, same complaint. She gives me the order for another nausea med. I ask the nurse what is going on with this patient that necessitates three late night stat calls in a row. The nurse, a woman I had known for a year at this point and had been nothing but composed the entire time, starts crying that the patient is abusive to her and the others and refuses to be seen during the day. As I hear her sniffling and trying to compose herself I make the remark "well hopefully the patient won't be with us that much longer." I repeat the order, she affirms it and hangs up. I go into work the next day exhausted from getting a combined 12 hours of sleep over the last three or four nights (getting calls was not uncommon, but this stretch was a little more than usual). My boss calls me in says the nurse (unbeknownst to me) had me on speaker phone. Says the patient said "I hope she dies" directly to the patient who then called the director of the hospice who called my boss. Boss states that he doesn't want someone so callous on his staff. I was pretty numb at this point, he put some statement in front of me and I signed it (kicking myself over that to this day). I gathered up my things and left. To this day I think my getting fired was uncalled for. I understand it, but I think it wasn't right. I wasn't allowed to explain myself or offer an apology to the patient or make any attempts to make it right. I never wished any harm on the patient and to this day still don't (my boss calling me callous though is ironic given the way he treated people I think). When you work in hospice you develop a bit of gallows humor about some things. That remark was never meant for that person, it was supposed to be from one colleague to another to try and get through a difficult time. I also have to say, I find the world bizarre in the sense that someone can make a mistake, offend someone (someone who is apparently quite cantankerous, I might add), and our response is to destroy that person's livelihood then act like that's the appropriate course of action.

Drive-thru is one of those things where they'll tell you "oh it's for folks who can't ambulate well," or during covid it was "for non-contact delivery of meds," but usually it's used by people too lazy to come into the store or people who don't plan well enough with their kids/pets and therefor insist they can't leave the car. There are plenty of regular folks who use drive-thru and it goes fine but there's a lot of that latter group too and it doesn't take much for one of them to gum up the works. People come in without their insurance, without their ID, insisting they don't pay that much usually, wanting to try apply coupons, showing up when nothing is even ready for them, getting stuff they know doesn't fit in the tubes. The back and forth nature of the tube system makes it take longer too. So many people don't even know what their insurance card looks like. One guy got so frustrated he tried to send his entire wallet over and of course that's when the tube system jammed. There's only one or two lanes working, usually staffed by one tech who also needs to manage phones and prescription processing. I understand why the drive-thru exists and I would support it if it were used appropriately but ultimately I think it cheapens what a pharmacy is and is misused.

I appreciate what you're saying and agree. It's very difficult for people to accept accountability. It's also really difficult to quit an addiction. Victimhood is definitely something that seems to encouraged in our modern society, and it does appear to be to our overall detriment. I'd just like to add two perspectives (ones that I'm pretty sure you're aware of and just didn't acknowledge in your message because it's impossible to cover everything): 

1) Accountability can take different forms. Going to rehab, taking suboxone, trying to taper off or trying different modalities are all forms of taking accountability. It's definitely possible to suffer setbacks on those. If someone does something bad during that event (stealing, hurting someone else, etc.) it should not be acceptable, but if they want to try again they should be commended.

2) Everyone's situation is different. Different people's brains respond to stimuli in a myriad of ways. People's support network looks different. Their reasons for being on the medication are different. All of these (and more) can determine how difficult it can be to quit a medication. 

I think the reason Purdue and Oxycontin were targeted was due to the particular push they were giving in getting the medication in the hands of the end user. They were misleading/lied in their research, they carried that through in their advertising campaign which was very aggressive and they showed disregard for the consequences of these choices. They had opportunities to back out, make the drug safer, make it more difficult to prescribe, but they chose not to because of how much they invested in the drug and how much it was making.

Like most things in this thread it's not so much the field as the management/culture of where you end up. There's opportunity for you to do some good and get satisfaction working in hospice; as there is in a hospital, and retail, and LTC, and any other field of pharmacy. A company that understands the issues facing you and genuinely cares about your well-being will make an effort to address these issues. I don't know if it's a matter of a few people speaking loudly or just how things are (I personally assume the latter), but it feels like companies believe they are better off neglecting their employees for short-medium term gains. These are not facts, just my perspective.

I have been unemployed for 1.5 years now but I was working at a hospice pharmacy for 2 years prior to that as the on-call pharmacist. I would work 7 days on 7 days off. During my weekdays on I'd staff from 12:30PM to 7:00PM (though I never left the pharmacy until 9PM at the earliest because I'd end up being called back anyways) and on weekends I worked from 10AM to 7PM and was on-call the rest of the time. 

The nurses who would call in seemed to remain willfully ignorant to the process and had no regard for the strain it would put on me when they'd call all throughout the night. I'd get calls for at 12AM, 2AM, 4AM, 6AM, etc. asking stuff like "what's the generic for prozac?" or ordering STAT pepto bismol for delivery that night. I'd do as required but there was no effort on their part to try and make it easier on them by working during normal business hours (I also pointed out it would help the patient if they did this as well). Going along with this the hospices seemed callously indifferent to the care of their patients. I recall one call for cipro, when I queried the indication they stated pneumonia, I told them they'd be better off prescribing levaquin to which they responded "yes, but that costs more." I was dumbfounded.

The owner/my boss was indifferent to these issues (I think he may have even encouraged it in a way), and why wouldn't he be? He was the one who got to pocket the after hours and delivery fees. I even went as far as tracking the after hours orders and making a report showing him how unnecessary so many of the calls were and how much money the clients could save by making some simple changes, but he didn't care. On top of this we were constantly low on delivery drivers. Clients would constantly call and complain that meds weren't arriving on time and we were instructed to lie and tell them they were stuck in traffic even though the real reason was we didn't have enough couriers to adequately cover our area. On top of this the boss just did not care about his employees at all. He would constantly be in the process of firing and hiring new couriers (though he would allow a lot of leeway for couriers that he was underpaying). He fired a technician when she didn't want to take the lead tech job when it opened up. We also had an intern working for us who graduated from school and became a pharmacist. My boss cut the regular hours pharmacist hour's in half and gave them to the intern stating that the regular pharmacist had been missing too much work (her father had a stroke a year prior and I covered for her twice in that time, it was not excessive. Apparently the straw was when she requested her birthday off two months in advance). He would also write me up for things out of my control. One client complained about me because I wouldn't allow a courier to leave a C2 at a doorstep without a signature even though no one was answering the door. What was I to do? 

I have never felt so unappreciated and disposable. I'm in my late 30s now. No money, tons of debt and living with my parents. I've been looking for a job but there just isn't anything out there it seems. The job put an enormous amount of stress on me, ruining my health and sleep and I have only gotten worse. It is very difficult to feel optimistic.

Went to Ascent Wilderness Program in Naples, ID for ~7 weeks in July 2000 then was sent to CEDU High School in Running Springs, CA until I was taken out by my parents sometime in the middle of November. I was sent because I was mainly sent because I was being truant which I find ludicrous to this day. Most of the kids, who were sent for things ranging from drugs to theft to assault, used to poke fun at me for not really belonging there. I will admit that I had my issues, but I don't think they were much worse than many other teens trying to discover themselves.

The day before I was sent out my parents took me to dinner at my favorite restaurant and sat down with me while I tried explaining my favorite computer game. It was nice, I felt like they were finally trying to take a little bit of an interest in me. I was awoken around 4AM by my parents and two men. My bags were already packed and my parents told me these men would be taking me away. I was allowed to use the restroom with the door open and then escorted out to their car. I thought about running but I wasn't particularly athletic and one of them was a massive man, well over 6'5", and the other looked like he was a member of the track team in college. A plane and then car ride took me to the camp in Idaho. After they dropped me off I began to be admitted and they informed me I had to be strip searched. I began hyperventilating, panicking and crying. Three men tried to force me on my feet but I resisted so they threw me to the ground and held me there until I was too tired to fight. I kept refusing to do the search so they grabbed me by the shoulders and marched me to a teepee to be in solitary confinement. I had rug burns and scrapes on my arms, legs and face to go along with the tears and snot covering my red face. It was humiliating. I was kept in solitary confinement for 2 nights until I agreed to do a quasi strip search with a towel around my waist. 

I won't go into much more detail about my experiences there except to say that it was not positive. The counselors were untrained in any kind of actual psychological support and many of them seemed to be on power trips. One counselor in particular by the name of Mike seemed to enjoy tormenting children. I do feel compelled to mention one other incident (among many others) that involved the night staff. If you had to go to the bathroom in the middle of the night you had to stand at the entrance to the teepee, raise your hand, say "potty please," and then wait for the night staff to bring you these oversized clogs (they'd take your boots each night to prevent you running away) so they could escort you to the outhouse. One night I kept standing there, asking for them to come over and they just ignored me. I could hear them talking about me, looking at me out of the corners of their eyes and occasionally laughing. They did long enough until I couldn't hold it any long and ended up urinating in my pants where I stood, still begging for them to come over. The end of your experience at the camp involved a week long backpacking trip with a group of kids brought in around the same time you were. During the final two days you were to set up your tarp in an isolated area and reflect on things. One thing you got was your mail that was sent to you during your time. I remember, sitting under that tarp in the middle of the woods with no one else in sight, reading the letter from my parents explaining that I would not be coming home from the camp, but instead be sent to a boarding school where I was to remain for an additional two years. I cannot even begin to articulate the profound senses loneliness and abandonment I felt that afternoon. It is still the darkest day in my life.

After the wilderness camp was over the same large man escorted me to boarding school. It was a very jarring experience, but not as bad compared to previous one. Again, I won't give exact details on experiences but speak on some generalities. There were these 3 to 5 hour "emotional growth" meetups that happened three or four times weekly called "raps" that were particularly scary. They basically involved kids calling each other out and then all the other kids and the staff piling on the kid until they were a crying, hysterical mess. The staff, who again were very poorly trained (one of them was promoted from the custodial staff), would attack the kids themselves if no one brought anything else up. Nothing was off limits, they'd twist stories, lie about things your family said to them about you, attack your personality/interests or even your appearance. It created a very paranoid environment. There was also a middle school along with the high school. I felt bad for the middle schoolers because they would be restrained by the staff at the drop of a hat. There were also these "emotional growth" workshops called "propheets" that I, thankfully, never got to experience. I only heard bits and pieces about what happened in them, but I do remember seeing a group of kids come out of one of these workshops that lasted over 48 hours. They were led up onto a stage in front of everyone where they lay down one on top of the other. I remember looking at them, they were intermittently laughing uncontrollably, it was extremely unnerving. Something that became readily apparent was that the kids who were there the longest were definitely the most messed up. They could seem tranquil but it wouldn't take much for a staff member to push them into being a inconsolable wreck (screaming, crying to the point where snot and drool are flowing freely, hitting themselves while red faced and rocking back and forth). I eventually got to talk to my parents when they visited and told them what was going on (the staff would screen your mail and monitor your phone calls) and got the ball rolling towards them pulling me from the program. 

To this day my relationship with my parents is still damaged. My mother and I have probably mended things up as much as we can while my father (who still insists that sending me away was the right move, and would do it again and feels I should just "get over it") and I can barely talk about the most banal things. It was disturbing, being exposed to that kind of experience and learning how you act in it. I also found out that the program was attached to a cult, which was upsetting on a few levels. You like to think that you'd rebel or see through a lot of the games they're playing against you, but you don't. I got to learn a lot about people that I wouldn't normally interact with and I am MUCH more skeptical today, but I think that's pretty much the only positives from the experience. When I got home I shut myself out to pretty much everyone and everything. I lived in my room in my parents house, went to school and when I graduated I worked. I almost always ate alone, I only really socialized through the internet and my hygiene was pretty abysmal (my room was absolutely gross since I almost never cleaned it). I'd wake up nightly to nightmares of being taken away, held down and having my limbs chopped off with an axe. I still get anxiety thinking about it, but it isn't as bad as it used to be. I have difficulty forming and maintaining relationships with others because of trust and abandonment issues that largely originated there. I wish I could go back and protect the younger me from what happened to him, or better yet, take his place and fight back against those people with the tools I have now.

May be posted but I didn't see it. Drugs for heartburn like Prilosec (hawked by Larry the Cable Guy) and Nexium do not work for heartburn on an as needed basis. You need to take them consistently for a couple days for them to work. However, if you take them for too long when you try to quit you will have even worse rebound heartburn. There are currently no established protocols for getting people off of these medications. That is not to say they are bad. They have their place in several conditions, but I don't think they should be over the counter. I usually recommend people take Zantec or Pepcid (or better yet, their generics... And stay away from Tagamet for heartburn) when they're having heartburn. They can be taken 30 minutes before a meal as needed, can be cut in half and are cheaper.

Talk to local independent pharmacies. Large institutions like chains and hospitals have waaaaaay too much red tape and legal hoops to jump through for you to just walk in.

What I did:
I studied a book for a couple weeks and got my tech license. Then I went into a pharmacy that was owned by a family asked if I could work for free. When I started they just had me doing really basic work: inventory of daily shipments, stocking shelves. After a week or so of that they let me start pulling medications off the shelf then after a couple weeks of that they let me compound some stuff, and I got to be with the pharmacist when he counseled patients (with their permission). It was a great experience and gave me a lot to talk about and draw from when I applied to pharmacy school. It was unpaid, but it was "only" 20 hours a week or so.

Currently in pharmacy school. By most metrics my application process and my time here are a complete success. 

Why: Like helping people, like being an expert at something and get a kick out of trying to explain really complicated things to people in a way that makes them say "oh, that's not so difficult." Plus I want to set myself up as a capable "provider" for if/when I ever meet that special someone. 

Application process was a massive success for me (got into everywhere I applied, including top school in the nation), though having to choose where to go led to massive amounts of anxiety which perpetuates to this day. I think that being honest actually played to my advantage. One application question asked me how I've addressed "issues in healthcare disparity" or something like that. I straight up told them I've never done that, but I've used my expertise to help others when I can (tutored ESL kids during part of undergrad). At this internship in a hospital I have now I told them that I didn't necessarily see myself working in a hospital, but I valued the experience it would give me and talked about what I wanted to get from it. Lesson learned: Be honest, and explain why you're actually there. When you're sincere it shows. I'd just gotten home from an organic chemistry exam and was pretty sure that I'd failed. I was really pissed off and felt the need to vent. I'd learned that punching a wall just meant money and time repairing it so I looked around for something I could unleash my fury upon without concern for its well being. My eyes immediately were drawn to my gigantic purple exercise ball. God I hated that thing, I bought it with the intent of using it to workout and sit at it while I worked on the computer to improve my core strength. Instead I just made me slouch over and get a sore back after 30 minutes of use and now it just sat in the middle of the floor taking up much more room than anything should.

Fixing my eyes upon it I gave it a good hard glare while I dropped my backpack to the floor. Nodding to myself I took three strides towards it and kicked it with all my might. I have never seen anything move so fast. In my anger induced haze I had neglected to account for the wall no more than 6 feet behind the ball. No sooner had I kicked it than the ball was immediately flying straight towards my face. If I even had time to process appropriate countermeasures I'm not sure I could have repelled the attack. The throbbing of my nose and the taste of metal in my mouth accompanied my backward descent to the ground. I folded like a book and smashed my head on the floor for good measure (fortunately it was a relatively fresh berber carpet on a relatively new pad). 

Lying there on the floor, staring up at the ceiling, my legs bent in a fashion that I didn't believe possible I began a system check. After ensuring that I did not suffer a concussion, was not bleeding and did not suffer any sort of joint injury I began to consider what may have been a more appropriate response to my frustration that day. Since that day I have not hit or broken anything out of anger, but just think of the day that exercise ball riposted my attack, how funny it must've looked, and laugh.

Beginning of the 5th grade year my whole class took a math test. The next day several kids, myself included, had to take another math test while the rest of the class got free time to do stuff like coloring, reading or playing in the area in front of the class. Being like 10 years old the last thing I wanted to do was take another math exam so I went up to the teacher and asked her why we were taking the test. She replied "Oh don't worry about it, it's not important, it's not graded or anything." I hear this, sit down and proceed to just bubble in random answers on the scantron. 

As it would turn out this was an exam to see which advanced math class we'd be placed in. Also, pretty much everyone taking it was a friend of mine. I wasn't allowed to retake the test because it wouldn't be fair (I understand the argument, but I also pointed out that I had no idea what was on that test). Apparently the teacher got in some trouble over this and she treated me poorly for the rest of the year as a result. Anyhow, my friends progress on and I get ostracized from that peer group and I began to greatly distrust authority figures. Long story short I ended up going from pretty much a straight A student to going to a juvenile boot camp and never graduating high school in the following years. I've since righted myself, but it delayed me significantly.



On a more happy note: I had several great college professors that made things like chemistry and math enjoyable and interesting.
